items.t: Son of Moses Baker; siblings Rachel, John, and Margaret.
Arrived single in DeWitt's Colony on August 13, 1830.
Received land on the Guadalupe River (title June 14, 1832) plus four town lots in Gonzales.
No marriage or occupation beyond farming is documented. His personality and appearance are entirely open.
Son of Jonathan and Margaret Cottle, who arrived in the colony July 6, 1829.
Received land at the head of the Lavaca River near Gonzales in 1832.
Married twice; his second wife was Nancy Curtis Oliver.
Rode as a courier warning of Mexican troop movements in September 1835, and fought at the Battle of Gonzales, October 2, 1835.
His exact birthplace is uncertain even to the historians who researched him. His occupation beyond landholding is unknown.
Born December 22, 1793, Woodford County, Kentucky; fought at the Battle of New Orleans in the War of 1812.
Married twice; left Missouri by wagon in 1830 and arrived in DeWitt's Colony January 10, 1831, with two sons.
Registered land on the Guadalupe above Gonzales, plus town lots.
Farmer and Indian scout; one of the "Old Eighteen" who refused to surrender the Gonzales cannon in September 1835.
A signed document proves he personally delivered 12 bushels of meal to the army's supply office.
Whether he ran a blacksmith shop is unconfirmed. The whereabouts of his wife and children later in the war are unrecorded.
Born Tennessee, around 1811, son of Henry Dearduff and Edna Thornhill.
Arrived March 20, 1830, single; received land on Sandies Creek plus town lots in Gonzales.
A frequent customer, starting in February 1835, at Joseph Martin's Gonzales store — buying clothing, food, and ammunition on credit.
No marriage is documented. His occupation beyond farming, his personality, and his reasons for later enlisting are entirely open.
A "John Davis" received land on Lavaca Creek in DeWitt's Colony on October 28, 1831, with a reputation as an "Indian fighter."
Voted in the 1835 Consultation delegate election.

This is a genuine identity puzzle, not just a thin record: researchers are not even certain the 1831 landowner is the same John Davis who later served in the militia, and warn he must be kept distinct from a different defender, John Gaston, with whom he has sometimes been confused.
Born in San Antonio, October 27, 1806, son of Erasmo Seguín.
After the Battle of Gonzales, Stephen F. Austin made him a captain and let him raise his own company — about 37 men at the start.
His company fought in the December 5, 1835 assault that captured San Antonio from Mexican forces.
Comes from a well-known San Antonio family active in local government for generations.
The exact size his company grew to, and its full membership by name, are not settled in the record.
Born San Antonio, May 26, 1782.
Postmaster of San Antonio from 1807 until nearly 1835.
Also served as alcalde, and was the only Texas delegate to the Mexican congress that wrote the Constitution of 1824.
Removed from public office at the start of the Revolution in 1835.
Father of Juan N. Seguín (above).
His day-to-day activity and personal reaction to being removed from office are not recorded.
Born José Salvador Ramón Flores de Abrego, into a San Antonio-area ranching family established since the 1700s.
Brother-in-law of Juan Seguín (his sister was Seguín's wife).
Served under Seguín from the earliest stages of the Revolution and also raised his own company of roughly 40 volunteers.
Praised by name, in a real surviving letter, by Stephen F. Austin on November 24, 1835, for his patriotism.
The exact size and full membership of his own company are not listed by name anywhere found.
Born San Antonio, January 1800.
Joined Juan Seguín's company of "Texas Mexicans" in early 1836.
His own memoir, told decades later, names a specific 22-man sub-unit of the company with its officers.
Known within his own community for his wide family and social connections.
His memoir was dictated in his late 70s, more than 40 years after these events — treat its most specific details as a good later account, not a document written at the time.
Born in San Antonio, descended from the original Canary Islander settlers of the town.
Married María de Jesús Olivarri in 1828; they had eight children.
Part of one of the wealthiest, most influential families in early San Antonio.
His activities in the fall of 1835 specifically, before his later company service, are not detailed anywhere found.

runs.t: *Roles: The Captain · The Scout · The Powder Man · The Youngest Rider · The Farrier*

items.t: Born 1782 in Virginia; a widower with two children when he moved to Texas from Missouri.
Settled in DeWitt's Colony in 1826; appointed deputy surveyor that same year and personally surveyed most of the land around Gonzales.
Opened a road from Béxar through Gonzales to Matagorda Bay in 1827.
Appointed colony surveyor by José Antonio Navarro in 1831.
Sent to negotiate with the Comanche in January 1836.
The names of his mother and sister, who came to Texas with him, are not recorded anywhere found.
Born March 9, 1819, Alabama — one of the most precisely documented ages in this whole roster.
Son of Silas and Sally (Taney) Fuqua, who arrived with a family of six on May 11, 1830.
His uncle, Benjamin Fuqua, also held land in the colony and served as a Consultation delegate (Company 6).
No occupation beyond farm family life is documented; no marriage (he was 16). His personality and appearance are undocumented.
Born around 1819, Kentucky.
Son of Rebecca (Warfield) Gaston and G.P.B. Gaston; his mother later remarried George Washington Davis (Company 6), making Davis his stepfather.
His sister Sidney Gaston married fellow Gonzales man John Benjamin Kellogg.
Family moved from Jefferson County, Kentucky, in 1831.
No occupation, marriage, or personal writing is documented.
Born Virginia (possibly Pennsylvania), 1802.
A sergeant under Lt. George Kimble.
Married Elizabeth Dearduff in 1821; they had five children.
Arrived in the colony February 20, 1830; held land on Plum Creek and town lots.
Sold provisions to the provisional government in December 1835 and was paid for wagon service.
His exact birthplace is disputed. His personality is undocumented.
Born 1796, Prince Edward County, Virginia (some records say Tennessee).
A merchant in Gonzales; owned a store, a home on Water Street, and "the only hotel in Gonzales."
Married Sidney Gaston in 1832; the marriage ended in separation the next year.
Served as road surveyor (1834) and as a town legal officer (1834).
One of the "Old Eighteen" cannon defenders, and a delegate to the Consultation in November 1835 (see Company 6).
The reason for his 1833 separation from his wife is not documented.
Arrived in DeWitt's Colony in January 1829.
Elected the first alcalde of Gonzales in November 1832; became judge for the whole colony in 1834.
One of the "Old Eighteen" who stood by the town's cannon in September 1835 — the Battle of Gonzales was fought on land he owned.
Appointed a captain in the Revolutionary Army at the Consultation in November 1835.
Never married.
His birth date, birthplace, and parents are entirely unknown. Nothing about his personal life beyond his public offices survives.
A gunsmith and blacksmith; one of the "Old Eighteen" defenders of the Gonzales cannon in September 1835, where he "made and repaired guns" for the town.
A veteran of the War of 1812 and earlier fighting before coming to Texas.
Wife Rachel Carpenter Sowell was born in 1785.
Family first settled in the town of Gonzales, later moving to the colony's western edge near present-day Seguin.
His exact arrival date in the colony, his personality, and his appearance are not recorded.
Born 1800, son of Levi and Mary (Sargent) Flanders.

A family story, repeated even by a major historical handbook but not otherwise confirmed, says he left Massachusetts after a dispute over foreclosing on a widow's mortgage and never contacted his family again.
Settled in Gonzales.
No marriage or children are documented. The estrangement story's factual basis has not been located — treat it as "traditional, not documented."
Born June 27, 1789, in colonial Virginia (present-day Brooke County, West Virginia).
Married Green DeWitt on December 15, 1808; they had six children.
A documented resident of the colony as of the 1828 census.
A "Come and Take It" flag with a cannon image flew at the Battle of Gonzales, and Gonzales women donated the cloth for a flag generally.

The popular story that Sarah and her daughter personally sewed that exact flag from a wedding dress is called "apocryphal" by one major historical source and repeated as fact by another — mark it "traditional, not documented." What is solid: a flag like that existed and flew; who actually sewed it is not settled.
Wife of Isaac Millsaps (Company 3).
From Pike County, Mississippi.
Her blindness and her seven children are documented facts, confirmed independently in more than one record.
Her exact marriage date, and the names and ages of her seven children, are not recorded. How or when she lost her sight is not documented — only that she was blind.
A widow when she married George C. Kimble (Company 3) on June 26, 1832.
Sources agree she had at least two children with him by 1836.

Her birth and death dates, her family background before marriage, and a fully agreed-upon list of her children are all unresolved between sources — like most Gonzales women in this record, she appears mainly through her husband's paperwork rather than anything documenting her own life.

items.t: Born October 12, 1797, near Philadelphia.
Landed in Texas February 12, 1831.
Married Rebecca Warfield Gaston (a widow) in 1820; her son John E. Gaston later served alongside his own stepson-in-law John B. Kellogg (both Company 3).
One of the "Old Eighteen" cannon defenders.
Secretary of the Gonzales Committee of Safety, 1835, and a Consultation delegate that November.
No specific committee votes or actions at the Consultation beyond "appointed a delegate" are recorded.
Born 1809 in Mifflin County, Pennsylvania, son of a War of 1812 officer and Pennsylvania legislator.
Graduated Jefferson College in 1835; trained as a surveyor.
Sailed from New Orleans, arriving in Texas in mid-December 1835.
A real surviving letter he wrote to his father from Gonzales, January 20, 1836, says: *"I have accordingly come on thus far with that intention as to connect myself with a Company of Rangers."*
No marriage or children are documented. Nothing beyond that one letter documents his personality.
Born September 24, 1790.
Co-founder of the colony; laid out the original Gonzales townsite starting in October 1825, as Green DeWitt's surveyor general.
Signed a treaty with the Karankawa people in 1827.
Served as a Texas Ranger major in 1835.
His personal relationships with the families whose land he surveyed are not recorded — only the survey paperwork itself.
Arrived in Texas July 6, 1829; registered for land in DeWitt's Colony May 1, 1831.
Married Louisa Cottle (sister of fellow Gonzales man George W. Cottle) in Missouri, 1826; they had four children.
One of the "Old Eighteen" cannon defenders, October 1835.
Registered a cattle brand on September 18, 1830.
His birthplace is a real, unresolved disagreement between sources. His children's names are not documented.
